prompt: On macOS or Windows, why is every path to running a container a virtual machine?

choices.text: Containers need a Linux kernel
choices.why: Right. A container is a Linux process. Docker Desktop hides that VM; lesson 1's Ubuntu VM shows it.

choices.text: Docker's licence forbids installing on those systems
choices.why: The licence asks larger companies for a subscription; it forbids no system.

choices.text: Go builds no binaries for macOS or Windows
choices.why: Section 04 builds both from one Linux machine.

choices.text: Their file systems are too slow for image layers
choices.why: Speed is not the reason; the kernel is.

prompt: Why does the lesson install Docker Engine from Docker's own repository?

choices.text: Ubuntu ships no container engine of any kind in its archive
choices.why: Ubuntu packages both `docker.io` and `podman`.

choices.text: Only Docker's packages run containers as root
choices.why: Running as root is a property of the daemon, not of who packaged it.

choices.text: Ubuntu's `docker.io` package lags behind
choices.why: Right. Docker's repository carries the current engine and the Compose and Buildx plugins.

choices.text: `apt` refuses unsigned packages from Ubuntu
choices.why: Ubuntu's packages are signed; the key in the commands is Docker's.

prompt: Match each package on the lab machine to what it gives.
What sets Podman apart from Docker Engine, as section 02 describes it?

choices.text: It reads a different file format instead of a Dockerfile
choices.why: `podman build` takes the same Dockerfile.

choices.text: It runs only on macOS
choices.why: Ubuntu packages it as `podman`.

choices.text: It builds Go binaries for other processors
choices.why: Cross-compiling is Go's job, in section 04.

choices.text: It has no daemon and is rootless by default
choices.why: Right. Its `build` and `run` take nearly the same flags as Docker's.

prompt: `docker ps` answers `permission denied while trying to connect to the docker API at unix:///var/run/docker.sock`. What is wrong?

choices.text: The daemon is not installed
choices.why: The socket exists; the user is refused it.

choices.text: The user is not in the `docker` group
choices.why: Right. Only root and the group `docker` open the socket.

choices.text: The image it asks for was never pulled to this machine
choices.why: `docker ps` needs no image at all.

choices.text: Docker Hub refused the request
choices.why: Docker Hub answers `429`; this message is the local socket.

prompt: Why does the lesson say membership of the `docker` group is root by another route?
hint: What does the daemon do for a member?

choices.text: The group's members share root's password
choices.why: No password is shared; the daemon acts for them.

choices.text: The group lets its members edit `/etc/sudoers` and grant themselves any command
choices.why: The group owns one socket, nothing in `/etc`.

choices.text: The root daemon mounts any host directory a member asks for
choices.why: Right. A container with `/` mounted reads every file root reads.

choices.text: Every container a member starts runs with the host's network and ports
choices.why: Containers get their own network unless told otherwise; the danger is the mount.

prompt: After `sudo usermod -aG docker $USER`, `docker ps` is still refused in the same terminal. Why?

choices.text: A running session keeps the groups it started with
choices.why: Right. Log out and in again, and the new group is there.

choices.text: `usermod` takes effect only after the Docker daemon restarts
choices.why: The daemon is untouched; the shell is what lacks the group.

choices.text: Group changes take about an hour to spread across the system
choices.why: There is no delay; the session simply started before the change.

choices.text: `-aG` removes every other group
choices.why: `-a` appends; it keeps the others.

prompt: Match each failure to its cause.

pairs.left: `failed to connect … check if the path is correct and if the daemon is running`
pairs.right: no daemon listening on the socket
Docker Hub's limit on anonymous pulls

pairs.left: no space left on the device
pairs.right: images and build caches piling up

prompt: Two environment variables choose the target of `go build`: `GOOS` for the operating system and ___ for the processor.
How many targets did `go tool dist list | wc -l` count?
Match each binary of the loop to the format `file` reported.
Built by the same loop, why did the `linux/arm64` binary come out static and the `linux/amd64` one dynamic?
hint: Which one was built for the machine it ran on?

choices.text: ARM processors forbid shared libraries
choices.why: ARM Linux uses shared libraries like any other Linux.

choices.text: Cross-compiling turns cgo off; the native build kept it on
choices.why: Right. There is no C compiler for the target, so cgo defaults to off there.

choices.text: The arm64 build used `-trimpath`
choices.why: The loop passed no flags; `-trimpath` removes paths, not libraries.

choices.text: The amd64 build ran out of memory while linking
choices.why: Both builds succeeded; the difference is cgo.

prompt: boxoffice has no C code. Why did the native build still link the C library?
hint: Two packages of the standard library.

choices.text: pgx is written in C
choices.why: pgx is pure Go.

choices.text: `net` and `os/user` use libc when cgo is on
choices.why: Right. `net` resolves names and `os/user` looks up users through the C library.

choices.text: Every Go binary on Linux needs libc to start
choices.why: `dist/try-static` starts with no libc at all.

choices.text: The race detector was compiled in
choices.why: No `-race` flag was passed to that build.

prompt: Match each build flag to what it does.

pairs.right: a static binary, with no C library
the machine's paths left out of stack traces
no symbol table and no debugging information
a string variable set at link time

prompt: A release script passes `-X main.verison=v1.0.0`, misspelt. What happens?

choices.text: The build stops with `undefined: main.verison`
choices.why: The linker does not complain about a name it never finds.

choices.text: The build succeeds and the binary says `dev`
choices.why: Right. The value goes nowhere, which is why the default is a word no release uses.

choices.text: Go creates the variable `verison` and sets it
choices.why: `-X` only sets a variable that already exists.

choices.text: `go vet` reports the typo before the build
choices.why: `go vet` reads source; the flag is never in the source.

prompt: After `-ldflags "-s -w"`, what happens when boxoffice panics?
hint: What goes is what a debugger needs.

choices.text: The panic prints no stack trace at all
choices.why: Stack traces use other tables, which stay.

choices.text: The process restarts itself
choices.why: Nothing in a Go binary restarts it; a supervisor does that.

choices.text: The trace shows addresses with no function names
choices.why: Function names remain in the trace.

choices.text: The panic still prints its stack trace
choices.why: Right. The symbol table and DWARF go; the tables a trace uses stay.

prompt: The plain static build was 26.0 MB. How many MB was the release build with `-trimpath -ldflags "-s -w …"`?
Which of these does `gcr.io/distroless/static-debian12:nonroot` contain?

choices.text: A shell, for `docker exec`
choices.why: There is no shell; section 06's `sh` failed to start.

choices.text: The C library, and the dynamic loader that links it in
choices.why: Their absence is why the dynamic binary failed.

choices.text: `apt`, so that packages are added to the image later
choices.why: No package manager is in it.

choices.text: CA certificates and time-zone data
choices.why: Right. Plus `/etc/passwd`, and a default user `nonroot`, uid 65532.

prompt: The dynamically linked binary in distroless fails with `exec /boxoffice: no such file or directory`. Which file is missing?
hint: Read the binary's header in section 04.

choices.text: `/boxoffice`, because `COPY` failed
choices.why: The binary is there; the message names it because it was executed.

choices.text: `/lib64/ld-linux-x86-64.so.2`, the loader
choices.why: Right. The header names that interpreter, and the image has no loader and no C library.

choices.text: `/etc/passwd`, which holds the image's users
choices.why: distroless has one; the kernel never got as far as users.

choices.text: `/bin/sh`, which the entrypoint needs in order to start
choices.why: The exec form of `ENTRYPOINT` uses no shell.

prompt: Why does the Dockerfile set `BOXOFFICE_HTTP=:8080`?

choices.text: Port 8080 is free only inside containers
choices.why: The port number is unchanged; the interface is the point.

choices.text: `EXPOSE` requires an `ENV` for every port
choices.why: `EXPOSE` only documents ports.

choices.text: Inside a container, `localhost` is the container itself
choices.why: Right. Listening on every interface is what lets a published port reach it.

choices.text: distroless forbids loopback addresses
choices.why: Loopback exists in every container; nothing outside reaches it.

prompt: What does `EXPOSE 8080 9090` do?

choices.text: Publishes both ports on the host
choices.why: That is `docker run -p`; gRPC stayed unreachable in section 07.

choices.text: Opens both ports in the host's firewall for incoming traffic
choices.why: A Dockerfile touches no firewall.

choices.text: Makes boxoffice listen on those two ports inside the container
choices.why: The `ENV` line does that, through lesson 14's configuration.

choices.text: Documents the ports and publishes nothing
choices.why: Right. `docker run` decides what reaches the host.

prompt: What `CONTENT SIZE`, in MB, did `docker image ls` report for `boxoffice:v0.16.0`?
In the container, pgx tried to connect with `user=` empty. Why?
hint: Where does pgx look when the URL names no user?

choices.text: The token file was mounted read-only
choices.why: The token has nothing to do with the database user.

choices.text: PostgreSQL refuses every connection that comes from inside a container
choices.why: The second run connected through the same socket.

choices.text: `TZ` was not set, so the connection string broke
choices.why: `TZ` changes timestamps, not the connection.

choices.text: Its `/etc/passwd` has no name for your uid
choices.why: Right. With `--user` set to your uid, the image knows no name to send; the URL has to carry one.

prompt: Match each thing boxoffice needs in the container to the `docker run` flag that gives it.

pairs.left: to be reachable from the host

prompt: The first container's log lines ended in `Z`. What did the second run add to show São Paulo time?
hint: The image has time-zone data and no local zone.

choices.text: A mount of the host's `/etc/localtime`
choices.why: No such mount was made; one variable sufficed.

choices.text: A rebuild with `-trimpath`
choices.why: `-trimpath` concerns paths, not time.

choices.text: `-e TZ=America/Sao_Paulo`
choices.why: Right. Go reads `TZ` and finds the zone in the image's time-zone data.

choices.text: A new `ENV` line in the Dockerfile
choices.why: The image was not rebuilt; the variable went on `docker run`.

prompt: Why did `database: migrating: …` come out at level `INFO` though `log.Fatalf` wrote it?

choices.text: Docker lowers the level of every line
choices.why: `docker logs` prints what the process wrote, unchanged.

choices.text: `slog.SetDefault` routes `log` calls at `INFO`
choices.why: Right. Every old `log` call becomes an `INFO` line: the `log` package has no levels, so its lines arrive at that one.

choices.text: The error was not fatal
choices.why: The process exited; only the level was wrong.

choices.text: `TZ` was missing
choices.why: The time zone changes the timestamp, not the level.

prompt: `docker stop boxoffice` took about a fifth of a second. Why so quick?

choices.text: Docker sends `SIGKILL` first
choices.why: It sends `SIGTERM` first and waits up to ten seconds before `SIGKILL`.

choices.text: distroless has no signals
choices.why: Signals belong to the kernel, not to the image.

choices.text: The container had served no requests
choices.why: It had served one, and the stop would be as quick with a hundred.

choices.text: boxoffice does nothing about `SIGTERM`
choices.why: Right. Go's default ends it at once and requests in flight are cut off; lesson 17 fixes that.

prompt: Why did `docker buildx build --platform linux/arm64` need no emulation?

choices.text: buildx emulates every platform for free
choices.why: Nothing was emulated at all here.

choices.text: arm64 and amd64 share one instruction set
choices.why: They differ; that is why the image fails on this machine.

choices.text: distroless contains an arm64 emulator
choices.why: distroless contains no programs at all.

choices.text: Nothing in the Dockerfile runs
choices.why: Right. Go already compiled for arm64; the build only copies `dist/boxoffice-linux-arm64` onto the arm64 distroless.

prompt: Running `boxoffice:v0.16.0-arm64` on the amd64 lab machine ended in which error?

choices.text: `no such file or directory`
choices.why: That was the missing loader, in section 06.

choices.text: `exec format error`
choices.why: Right. The kernel was handed an arm64 program on an amd64 processor.

choices.text: `permission denied`
choices.why: That was the socket, in section 03.

choices.text: `429 Too Many Requests`
choices.why: That is a registry's answer, not the kernel's.

prompt: In the two-stage Dockerfile, what does `FROM --platform=$BUILDPLATFORM golang:1.27.1 AS build` achieve?

choices.text: The build stage runs natively
choices.why: Right. Go cross-compiles from there; emulating the target for the whole build would be many times slower.

choices.text: It copies the Go toolchain into the final image
choices.why: `COPY --from=build` takes one file; the toolchain stays behind.

choices.text: It pulls the image without Docker Hub's limit
choices.why: The flag picks a platform; the lab's pull still got `429`.

choices.text: It turns cgo on for the build
choices.why: The stage sets `CGO_ENABLED=0`.

prompt: Which statements match this lesson? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: `go version -m` reads back how a binary was built
choices.why: Right. It showed `-trimpath=true`, `CGO_ENABLED=0` and the target.

choices.text: `.dockerignore` keeps the build context to the release binaries
choices.why: Right. It ignores everything and lets `dist/boxoffice-linux-*` back in.

choices.text: The image runs boxoffice as root
choices.why: The `nonroot` tag makes the default user `nonroot`, uid 65532.

choices.text: `CGO_ENABLED=0` was the fix for the loader error
choices.why: Right. A static binary needs no loader.

choices.text: Cross-compiling for Windows needed a Windows SDK
choices.why: Go needed nothing installed beyond itself.

prompt: Order the steps from source to a serving container, as this lesson took them.
items: `docker run` with the port, the socket, the user, the token and the URL

prompt: A teammate's boxoffice image fails in distroless with `exec /boxoffice: no such file or directory`. What do you check first?

choices.text: Whether `COPY` put the binary at `/boxoffice`
choices.why: The message names the program even when it is there.

choices.text: Whether port 8080 is published
choices.why: The process never started; ports are not involved.

choices.text: Whether the `docker` group exists
choices.why: The daemon ran the container; the failure is inside it.

choices.text: Whether the binary was built with cgo on
choices.why: Right. `file` or `ldd` on it shows a loader, and `CGO_ENABLED=0` is the fix.
